paragraphs.text: 1 The fool hath said in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, and have done abominable iniquity: there is none that doeth good. 2 God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, that did seek God.
The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.
They are corrupt, and have done abominable iniquity.
There is none that doeth good [1].

The word "fool" here, "nabal," does not mean mere foolishness, that is, lack of knowledge or lack of wisdom; rather it carries moral corruption, especially in resisting faith in God and rejecting His will in folly. As it came in (Psalm 74:22): "Arise, O God, plead thine own cause: remember how the foolish man reproacheth thee daily." The righteous Job called his wife, who murmured at what the Lord allowed, "one of the foolish women" (Job 2:10). It is said of the fool: "The vile person (nabal) shall be no more called liberal, nor the churl said to be bountiful. For the vile person will speak villany, and his heart will work iniquity, to practise hypocrisy, and to utter error against the LORD" (Isa 32:5-6).
The "fool" here means a trivial, reckless, base person. A man whose head is full of mire and whose heart is defiled, who walks in darkness.

"There is no God": this expression is not to be taken in its literal sense, that every fool is an atheist who denies the existence of God; rather it means here practical atheism, where some do not deny the existence of God but deny His divine providence, and if they do not deny it with their tongues, then in their hearts and inner thoughts they see in God the harsh Being who lies in wait for man to punish him for every sin or weakness in his life.

* Who thinks rightly and does not know that God exists?! But it happens again and again that, although the truth obliges us to acknowledge God, evil pleasures urge us to deny the existence of God, so we utter in our hearts the counsel of evil in order to accept it, that which is opposed to faith.

* He who dares to say that there is no God is without understanding and a fool. This is the mark of Rabsaris and Rabshakeh, for they spoke thus: "Have the gods of the nations delivered their lands and those who worship them, so how will your God protect you and protect your city?!" But in their hearts and conscience they said that there is no God. The prophet, by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, had already known what was in their conscience (2 Kgs 18).
And we also say that those who deny the divinity of Christ are fools, because their aim is to nullify His manifest great works that prove His divinity.
And also those who say: Yes, God exists, the Creator of the beginning, but He does not care for it; these rely on human power, and they are fools.

* He who falls into foul deeds says in his heart: "There is no God," and goes out of the true faith, and falls into unbelief, because by his abominations he corrupts what God has sown in the hearts of men of right belief and sound opinion. For faith does not exist except with works, as Cornelius and others, because of the purity of their conduct and the goodness of their works, were enlightened with the light of the upright faith; but whoever is opposed to that is corrupt.
* Corruption begins with evil belief, then morals are removed, and after that the most wicked evils are done; these are the steps..
Corrupt are these men and defiled with iniquities. They say: "If he be the Son of God, let him come down from the cross." See, they say openly: "He is not God."

"They are corrupt, and have done abominable iniquity: there is none that doeth good." The author of the Psalm speaks of the general corruption that has come upon mankind since the fall of Adam and Eve. "And God looked upon the earth, and, behold, it was corrupt; for all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth" (Gen 6:12).

The Psalm uses the word "Elohim," that is, God the Creator. If the peoples refused to enter into a covenant with Him, and did not accept His dwelling in their midst, then as a Creator who loves His creation, He looks upon all the children of men, that perhaps they may understand His attributes as a lover of mankind and seek Him. As it came in Psalm 33: "The LORD looketh from heaven; he beholdeth all the sons of men. From the place of his habitation he looketh upon all the inhabitants of the earth" (Ps 33:13-14). If the fruit of ignorance or folly is that man thinks God is isolated in His heavens, not caring about the sons of men, the psalmist, on the other hand, brings out that God in His humility uses human expressions. He looks upon the human race in order to pour into them understanding and wisdom, so that they may perceive His mercy and accept to enter into a covenant with Him.

By saying: "They have turned back together," the psalmist brings out the collective action, as though mankind had agreed together to turn back from God their Creator and the One who cares for them. Mankind rejected the divine truth, and agreed together to walk in crooked ways.
God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see:
If there were any that did understand, that did seek God. [2]

St. Augustine sees that this phrase raises a question: does God not know everything, that He looks down from heaven to see? He answers this question that Holy Scripture often refers to the works of God in a human way for our sake. When it says: "For the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God" (1 Cor 2:10), it does not mean that the Spirit needs to search in order to know the deep things of God, but this was written so that we ourselves may long to search the divine mysteries by the Holy Spirit of God. Thus when it says here that God looks down from heaven upon the sons of men, and finds them all corrupted, God was not unaware of this; rather the aim of this expression is to declare to mankind their true state, and that every man may seek salvation from the corruption that has come upon him as upon his brothers.
Every one of them is gone back together, they are corrupt, there is none that doeth good, no, not one [3].

The word "gone back" or "turned backward" shows that man was created upright by God, but by his will he deviated from uprightness and was disabled, because he disabled the sovereignty given to him by God, and submitted like a slave to shameful passions. He disabled the keenness of his insight, since he came to prefer evil to good.

St. Augustine says that by this He prepares every man to enjoy the divine work; for if all the sons of men are corrupt, God does not hasten to pass judgment on them, but works to raise up from the sons of men sons for Himself. This is what St. Augustine affirms in his interpretation of this Psalm! If men did not enjoy sonship to God, the condition of the corrupt sons of men would be thus: "There is none that doeth good, no, not one."

* Before the appearing of Christ, the Word of God in the flesh, the darkness of Satan, with sin and disobedience, was throughout all the earth without light, and as the prophet David says in the thirteenth psalm and the fifty-second psalm: "The Lord looked down from heaven to see if there were any that did understand or seek God, and there was not one" (Ps 14:2; Ps 53:3). But when Christ the Word of God became incarnate, the Light begotten of the Father without separation from Him, like the ray from the sun, and gave us through Baptism the Holy Spirit, He shone upon us and stirred His fear in us, and truly made known in our hearts the light of His promises, until we believed Him and kept Him and loved Him and kept His commandments.

entries.section: 3. They eat up the people of God as bread

paragraphs.text: 4 Have the workers of iniquity no knowledge? who eat up my people as they eat bread: they have not called upon God. 5 There were they in great fear, where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee: thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them.
Have the workers of iniquity no knowledge? who eat up my people as they eat bread: they have not called upon God. [4]

Here the speaker is God Himself, who offered to mankind what satisfies all their needs. He created everything on earth and under the earth for man to enjoy. And above all He offered them Himself, to satisfy their depths with Himself and His surpassing love. But man in his greed wishes to devour his brother. As it was said in the Book of Jeremiah: "Pour out thy fury upon the heathen that know thee not, and upon the families that call not on thy name: for they have eaten up Jacob, and devoured him, and consumed him, and have made his habitation desolate" (Jer 10:25). As it was said: "Their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly" (Hab 3:14). "Who also eat the flesh of my people, and flay their skin from off them; and they break their bones" (Mic 3:3).
What happens to the righteous who are devoured by the wicked?

St. Augustine answers: [This people who are devoured, this people who suffer from the wicked, who groan and are in pain in the midst of the wicked, now become children of God instead of being sons of men; thus they have been devoured (as sons of men).]
And what of the wicked?

St. Augustine often repeats that human wolves, when they devour human lambs and drink their blood, are changed from ravening wolves into gentle lambs, as happened with Saul of Tarsus. The wicked want to devour people and swallow them continually and without ceasing, as they eat bread daily, but as they eat them, some of them become sons of God by accepting the faith and enjoying baptism.
* This people who suffer from the wicked are devoured, this people who sigh and are in pain in the midst of the wicked; by this they are devoured.
When the Assyrians besieged Jerusalem they did not regard God but insulted Him, therefore He sent His angel to terrify them (2 Kgs 18).

He who does not call upon God for God Himself, but for temporal things, loses his joy in the gladness of salvation, and instead of peace fear comes upon him without any real cause except his deprivation of God, the source of peace.

* Some call, but they do not call upon him of whom it is said: "They have not called upon God" (Ps 53:4). They call, but they do not call upon God. You call what you love; you call what you are drawn to. So if you call upon God for this reason, that money may come to you; that you may receive an inheritance, or that a worldly rank may come to you, then you are calling upon these things which you desire to come to you, and you make God a helper to fulfill your lusts, not one who listens to your needs. What if you desire something evil? Would He not be merciful to you and not give it to you? And when He does not give it to you, God becomes nothing to you, and you say: How many times have I prayed, I have prayed often but He does not hear!
* It is fitting for us to call upon God, asking Him not for His temporal blessings, but seeking Him for His own person.
Do these not call upon God daily? They do not call upon God.

Take heed: if I am able to tell you, with the help of God Himself, that God must be worshipped freely (and not for the sake of good things), to be loved for His own sake freely, that is, loved with purity, not to give something, but to give Himself. He who wants God to be absent does not call upon God.
There were they in great fear, where no fear was: for God hath scattered the bones of him that encampeth against thee.
Thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them [5].

"Thou hast put them to shame": if God allows the wicked to trouble His people and His believers, it is only for a time, but "He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision. Then shall he speak unto them in his wrath, and vex them in his sore displeasure" (Ps 2:4-5).

And as the Lord said by the tongue of Isaiah concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria: "Whom hast thou reproached and blasphemed? and against whom hast thou exalted thy voice, and lifted up thine eyes on high? even against the Holy One of Israel. By thy messengers thou hast reproached the Lord, and hast said, With the multitude of my chariots I am come up to the height of the mountains... But I know thy abode, and thy going out, and thy coming in, and thy rage against me. Because thy rage against me and thy tumult is come up into mine ears, therefore I will put my bridle in thy nose, and I will turn thee back by the way by which thou camest" (2 Kgs 19:22-23, 27-28).
The Assyrians were at ease and in safety, and behold, terror fell upon them, and a hundred and eighty-five thousand soldiers perished among them (2 Kgs 19:35).

There was nothing to cause fear in the Lord Christ, who came to save the world, not to set up a temporal kingdom for Himself, and yet Herod was terrified and plotted to kill Him, and the Jewish leaders were terrified of Him and asked for His crucifixion.
St. Augustine sees that he who calls upon God does not fall into terror where there is nothing to cause real terror, for he says:
[Is there fear if a man loses riches? There is no fear, and yet men fear in this case. But if a man loses wisdom, then rather there is fear, and yet they do not fear...
You fear lest you return the money (which God gave you), and you want to lose salvation.]
"For God scattereth the bones of them that please men" [5]

He who does not call upon God fears where fear is not needed, because he cares to please his body and his lusts and also men, not God; but he who calls upon God fears no one but God, whom he seeks to please. The first, since he seeks to please men, is shattered, and loses his spiritual temple, and his bones are scattered.

* God scatters the bones of those who please men (Ps 53:5). By bones he does not mean here those of the body, for there is no example of a person whose bones are scattered in this way. Rather he means here the power of the mind and heart by which man can practice righteousness. These powers of the soul are the zeal that leads to earnest perseverance, spiritual maturity, patience and endurance. These traits God scatters in those who please men.

* He scatters the bones of those who please men... because the desire to please men is always the food of the accursed pride which God hates as men do, and it is the head and root of pride. He who falls victim to this passion desires honor and praise, and this is a thing God hates, for He hates the proud, but He receives the one who is humble in his thought, who does not seek glory, and shows him mercy.

* (The believer) must offer thanksgivings to God, the awesome, glorified, holy. And he must do nothing in a spirit of contention and vainglory (Phil 2:3), but for the glory of God and His good pleasure. "For God scattereth the bones of them that delight in evil" (Ps 53:5).

* The Apostle warns us, saying: "Let us not be conceited" (Gal 5:26). And the Lord rebukes the Pharisees, saying: "How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from the only God?!" (Jn 4:44) And of these also the blessed David speaks in warning: "The Lord hath scattered the bones of them that flatter men" (Ps 53:5).

* The soldier of Christ who desires to strive lawfully in this true spiritual battle must strive by every means to conquer this unsound, fickle, many-formed being, which, when it attacks us from every side like various manifold evils, we can escape by such a remedy as this: thinking of David's saying: "The Lord hath scattered the bones of them that flatter men" (Ps 53:5). At the beginning we must not allow ourselves to do anything out of conceit or to gain any vainglory. Likewise when we have begun something well, we must strive to strengthen it with the same care, lest the disease of vainglory creep in upon us and bring to nothing all the fruit of our labors.

* If you wish that no one should molest you, entreat God in secret and fast, and nothing will harm you. If the demons tell you to please men, do not accept, and remember what the Lord said: "Take heed that ye do not (your good deeds) before men, (but) in secret; and your Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward you openly" (Mt 6:1-4). And if Satan urges you to work to please men, look at the saying of the prophet: "God will scatter the bones of them that please men, He will put them to shame, for God despiseth them" [(Ps 53:5) cf. the Septuagint], and He does not listen to their prayer, but rather is wroth with them.

* "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven." If He had said only: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works," it would have seemed that He made the praise of men the aim, which is what the heretics seek, and those who ask for honors and those who rush after passing glory. It was said of these groups: "For if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10), and the prophet says of those who pleased men: "Thou hast put them to shame, because God hath despised them," and "because God hath scattered the bones of them that please men" (Ps 53:5), and the Apostle says: "Because you are conceited" (Gal 5:26), as he says: "But let every man prove his own work, and then shall he have rejoicing in himself alone, and not in another" (Gal 6:4).

entries.section: 4. The Church's rejoicing in spiritual freedom

paragraphs.text: Oh that the salvation of Israel were come out of Zion.

entries.section: 4. The Church's rejoicing in spiritual freedom

paragraphs.text: When God bringeth back the captivity of his people, Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad [6].

If ignorance causes the community (like a member) to lose its faith in God and its spiritual conduct so that it lives in corruption, not calling upon God for His own sake but seeking what is temporal, so that its bones are scattered and it loses its peace and even its very being, then salvation gives the Church freedom from the captivity of the devil, so she is filled with joy and rejoicing.

Father Anthimus of Jerusalem sees that the word "Israel" here is applied to every believer who beholds God with his mind, and the word "Jacob" is applied to everyone who wrestles with and pursues the enemy. It is as though the rejoicing Church is she who sees by faith God her Savior, and strives by the grace of God in her battle against the devil her enemy.

The expression "God bringeth back the captivity of his people" does not mean the Babylonian captivity, but the return of the people to their former glory after the enemy had humbled them for a time. This is what Holy Scripture meant when it spoke of the captivity of Job (Job 42:10), where the Lord restored him to his former glory before he entered into the trial.

Bringing back the captivity means return to glory and honor, as it came (Ezek 16:53; Zeph 2:7; Amos 9:14; Hos 6:11). If sin humbles man and brings the soul as into captivity, then repentance, or returning to God, grants release from captivity, and the enjoyment of rejoicing with honor and glory.
Fruitful Sufferings
* On the cross, O Savior, You accepted the sufferings of love, and You travailed with us, Your Church and Your children!
You granted us to share Your sufferings, that we too may travail with new children, formed in Your likeness!
* You allowed the wicked to devour us like bread, so that they might be changed from sons of men into sons of God!
They devour us every day without ceasing, and You turn the affliction into a fruitful witness to the truth!
* The wicked do not call upon You, because they do not know You, so they are deprived of inner peace, and are terrified without cause!
But we see You, and we strive by Your grace, we are freed from the authority of the enemy, and we enjoy constant joy and heavenly rejoicing!

1 O God, my heart is fixed; I will sing and give praise, even with my glory. 2 Awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early. 3 I will praise thee, O LORD, among the people: and I will sing praises unto thee among the nations. 4 For thy mercy is great above the heavens: and thy truth reacheth unto the clouds. 5 Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: and thy glory above all the earth.
The psalm begins with a hymn of praise to God, in which the psalmist finds refuge and steadfastness in the heart of God. It is a hymn of victory over all the troubles of danger.
O God, my heart is fixed.
I will sing and give praise,
even with my glory [1].
The Septuagint and Coptic versions read: "My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready. I will sing and chant praise in my glory".
* "My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready." I am ready not only in deed, but also in heart and mind. My heart is ready in desire; my heart is ready to serve by deed [3].

* "I will sing and chant praise in my glory." Simply, it means that when I praise You with a melody, O Lord, when I chant to You, I offer You no benefit; it is for me alone. In truth, another psalm says: [You have no need of my goodness] (See Ps 16:2). Therefore what I do, I do for my own good. When I serve You, this is a glory to me.
We fast; do we give God anything? We do this for the sake of our sins.

We sleep on sackcloth. What does God do with this? Only one thing: we save our souls, and this is what He desires. As a good and gentle physician rejoices in his patient when he heals him, so our Lord does [4].

St. Jerome *The prophet repeated the words "my heart is ready" twice, because if one who is determined to receive a king in his house prepares two things, first cleaning it of filth, and second adorning it with the most precious and finest furnishings, so also he who is about to receive Christ at once into his heart must cleanse it by confessing his sins, and beautify it with the adornment of good and righteous works. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God, and they praise and chant to Him in their glory, I mean in their intellectual and practical virtues, which glorify and honor them in this world and in the next. Also their glory will be Christ, who, when He took what is ours, made us the like of His image and partakers of His glory.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem
Awake, psaltery and harp:
I myself will awake early [2].
The Septuagint and Coptic versions read: "Awake, my glory! Awake, psaltery and harp! Awake at the time of dawn".

The psalmist wants to praise God at dawn, before the rising of the sun, affirming that the night did not hinder him from thinking about God's dealings with His people as well as with himself personally, so he offers the firstfruits of his day to praise and thanksgiving to God.

St. Jerome sees that the address here is also from the incarnate Son to the Father. By His incarnation the Word of God declares that He bears the harp of His becoming man, on which to play the melody of divine love toward all mankind. His soul went down to Hades playing the melody of victory, releasing the souls of those who had fallen asleep in hope, freeing them from bondage, and leading them to Paradise.
* As the psaltery has many strings, and if one string is broken the whole instrument becomes useless, so also in our deeds: if we disobey one commandment, our psaltery is broken [5].

* If you are a psaltery, if you are a harp, why are you silent and do not glorify God? "Awake at the time of dawn." There is no blessing or praise of God in darkness, but in light. I want to say something awesome. Even if we rise in the night, it is to bless God in the light. For the Christian has no night, but the Sun of Righteousness is always shining for him [6].

* According to another interpretation, the Lord Himself says: "My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready. I am ready here; and I am ready in the world to come. I am a Savior on earth; and I am a Savior in heaven. I give eternal life to both angels and men. "Awake, psaltery and harp." The Lord speaks to His body: Psaltery and harp, you who went down to Hades and rested, awake and glorify the Lord. Be sure that you understand what I say. It is not he who holds the psaltery and harp who praises, but the psaltery and harp themselves praise the Father. It is the Father, who is blessed and praised by others, whereas the body (of Christ) and His humanity that He took praise the Lord [7].

St. Jerome *By saying, "Awake, my glory," he urges and raises up the spirit of prophecy that was in him to glorify Him with spiritual glory. And by saying psaltery and harp he raises up the powers of his soul and the senses of his body, so that both sides may agree in praising God in harmony and union, and for receiving the Holy Spirit. He also raises up the Old and New Testaments, so that in one accord they may proclaim the works of the incarnation of our Lord. For the Old Testament contains foreknowledge of what was to be, while the New Testament proclaims the fulfillment of the prophecies. His saying "early" makes clear the time at which the Sun of Righteousness, who is our Lord Jesus Christ, arose; I mean the time of His incarnation, because David from that time until the end praises and chants to God with us who have been enlightened and who walk as in a good day.
Hesychius said: When the prophet urged Christ, saying, "Awake, my glory," our Lord's answer to him is, as it were: Yes, I awake, and I rise from the dead as from an early sleep.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem
I will praise thee, O LORD, among the people: and I will sing praises unto thee among the nations [3].
The Septuagint and Coptic versions read: "I will confess You among the peoples, O Lord, and I will chant to You among the nations".

*It is as though the psalmist joins us who believe in Christ, for when we recite what he sings, he has praised and chanted to God with us among the peoples concerning the salvation that the Lord Christ accomplished.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem
For thy mercy is great above the heavens: and thy truth reacheth unto the clouds [4].
The Septuagint and Coptic versions read: "For Your mercy is great above the heavens, and Your truth unto the cloud".

* There is no creature that does not depend on God's tenderness. Each one of us needs God's compassion. Gabriel and Michael, the seraphim and cherubim, the powers and authorities, all are truly holy, yet they stand in need of the mercies of their Creator. I am not belittling the angels, but proclaiming their Creator, for the angels themselves offer Him glory of their own free will and with joy.

We can also express the thought carried by this phrase in another way: Your tenderness lifts us from earth to heaven. "And Your truth unto the clouds"... How does God's truth reach heaven? The Son of God says: "I am the way, the truth, and the life" (Jn 14:6). And He came down to earth and conversed with men (Bar 3:38). How then is God's truth in the clouds? It is quite clear that the prophet is referring to the apostles and the saints.
"Great above the heavens." God is not magnified on earth. For as long as we are earthly we do not magnify God, but when we are changed from earthly to heavenly we magnify God [8].

St. Jerome *His saying, "Your mercy is great above the heavens and unto the clouds," means that Your mercy is wider and broader than the heaven, and covers all our sins from above. And that the beginning of mercy is on earth and its end is in heaven.
I mean that You show mercy to the people who are on earth, as it is written that the earth is full of Your mercy, and the end of those who are shown mercy is to reach heaven.

As for his saying "unto the clouds" concerning the prophets and apostles, it is because they are lofty and noble, and because God rains down His teachings to water people through His apostles and prophets...

The prophet's saying, "Your mercy is great in the heavens," means that the angels magnify His divinity above the heavens. Also, He revealed His greatness and majesty to all when You ascended into the heavens, for humanity veiled Him when You were on earth; I mean, before Your ascension to heaven people did not know the greatness of Your divinity. But now they know that You are a great God in the heavens and glorified.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem
Be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens: and thy glory above all the earth [5].
In the spirit of prophecy the psalmist saw the Lord Christ ascending into heaven, and his soul rejoiced, sharing with the disciples who returned from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem with great joy.
The psalmist realized that he shares in praise with the men of the New Testament, for he now has a store laid up in heaven.
By the ascension of the Lord Christ, the Head of the universal Church, the whole body, made up of God's people in the Old and New Testaments, gained the right to go forth to heaven.
The psalmist realized that he was in wondrous glory, for he was being raised from the dust and the dunghill to sit with the nobles of the nobles of his people, that is, with the heavenly orders.
*This saying contains a prophecy of the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ into the heavens.
*By His ascension and the sending of His Holy Spirit He saved His beloved, I mean the people for whose sake, out of His love for them, He came down and became incarnate and saved them from Satan.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem

entries.section: 2. God the hope of His people

paragraphs.text: 6 That thy beloved may be delivered: save with thy right hand, and answer me. 7 God hath spoken in his holiness; "I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth. 8 Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine; Ephraim also is the helmet of my head; Judah is my sceptre. 9 Moab is my washpot; over Edom will I cast out my shoe; O Philistia, shout aloud over me." 10 Who will bring me into the strong city? who will lead me into Edom? 11 Wilt not thou, O God, who hast cast us off? and wilt not thou, O God, go forth with our hosts? 12 Give us help from trouble: for vain is the help of man. 13 Through God we shall do valiantly: for he it is that shall tread down our enemies.

Despite the dangers through which the people pass, their hope in God pours upon them a spirit of joy, not only upon obtaining victory, but from the moment the calamity begins. For God, as the leader of His people, carries them across to certain victory. The people rest and hide amid dangers in the heart of God, which is wide with love.
That thy beloved may be delivered:
save with thy right hand, and answer me [6].

entries.section: 2. God the hope of His people

paragraphs.text: *Therefore the Church says by the tongue of the elect: "His left hand is under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me" (Song 2:6). The Church rests her head under God's left hand, as though meaning by this the good things of earthly life, and she rests on them with the joy of surpassing love. But God's right hand, which embraces her, means that eternal joy surrounds her on every side. Therefore Solomon also says: "Length of days is in her right hand; and in her left hand riches and honour" (Prov 3:16). Here Solomon shows that riches and honor appear as though inscribed on the left hand. So the psalmist says: "Save with thy right hand, and answer me" (Ps 108:6). Here he refers to the right hand, because he means that he asks for eternal salvation. Therefore it is also written: "Thy right hand, O LORD, hath dashed in pieces the enemy" (Ex 15:6). God's enemies may enjoy good things by God's left hand, but God's right hand destroys them. For we usually see the wicked exalted in earthly life, but at the coming of eternal glory the curse falls upon them [9].
God hath spoken in his holiness;
I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth [7].

This salvation does not only gladden the hearts of the believers, but God Himself says: "I will rejoice." He delights in the salvation of mankind, and in the victory of the believers there is glory for Him, for He rejoices in them and in their victory through Him.

St. Jerome sees that the secret of the psalmist's praise and the exultation of his heart is God's delight in salvation. There is nothing in which the Father delights as He does in the Cross of the Lord of glory Jesus, where divine love was realized in its most splendid form. The Father rejoiced in the Cross of His only-begotten Son.

The works of the Cross and its efficacy remain the secret of our constant praise, where we find our happiness in sharing with the Crucified the sufferings of love, and in being lifted up by the Cross above every temporal concern.
St. Jerome also sees that the manifold fruits of the Cross have become the song that he sings:

a. I will divide Shechem: St. Jerome sees that Shechem means "shoulders"; if the Lord Christ in His love bent His back to carry the Cross on His shoulders for us with all joy, He granted us also to carry the Cross with Him on our shoulders as a sweet and joyful yoke.

b. I will mete out the valley of tents (Succoth): where Christ grants His saints who have enjoyed His Cross the knowledge of His mysteries while still on earth, but each according to his stature or measure.

* "God hath spoken in his holiness," whether in the temple, or in one of His saints, or in the prophet. He was heard in Moses, and was heard in the Apostle, and truly I say He has spoken in His Son. What did God promise? What followed: "I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem." He says: For this I was crucified, that I may distribute Shechem. "Shechem" in our language means "shoulders." And shoulders, on the other hand, are used for work. The meaning then: the purpose of my crucifixion is to share my work with my saints. For this I was crucified, to put my sweet yoke and my light burden on the shoulders of men. This You do, O Lord, as You promised; You are glorified and Shechem is divided [10].

* "And mete out the valley of tents." Truly our Lord and Savior entered this valley of tears, the place of our humility, in this world. Yet the saint in this world still does not know what befits him as he ought, "for we know in part, and we prophesy in part" (1 Cor 13:9) [11].

St. Jerome *The spiritual meaning is that "Shechem" is interpreted "the exalted." The One exalted above worldly things is the Holy Spirit, who divided His gifts among the believers after the ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ into heaven, and measured and apportioned them to each one according to his worthiness.

As for the valley of shadows (Succoth), it is said of the whole inhabited world, in which the lands are pitched like tents; He made them portions for the heads of the churches, that each one may manage what his church comprises.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem
Gilead is mine; Manasseh is mine;
Ephraim also is the helmet of my head;
Judah is my sceptre [8].

St. Jerome sees that the Lord Christ rejoices also in the fruit of His Cross, for He has gained great riches, not out of need of anything, but for the sake of the salvation of mankind and its enjoyment of what is to come:

a. "Gilead is mine": since Gilead means "emigration," the Gentiles emigrated to Him, or returned to Him after living in the humiliation of bondage to the devil. They returned with the spirit of freedom, rejoicing, and their Savior rejoiced over them.
b. "Manasseh is mine": for it had previously forgotten God's fatherhood to it. And now it has returned to Him, remembering His love for it.
c. "Judah is my sceptre": mankind came to be in royal glory, belonging to the King of kings, after it became "Judah," that is, "confession," confessing the mercies of God who forgives sins.

* "Gilead is mine, Manasseh is mine." Our Lord and Savior rejoices, because He has much wealth. The meaning of "Gilead" is "emigration." He rejoices because the Gentiles have emigrated to Him. "Manasseh" means "forgetfulness," and accordingly we understand: this son who took his inheritance and squandered it and forgot all that concerns me remembers me now. I call him Manasseh, that is, from forgetfulness, because he forgets but returns to his father.

"Ephraim" is interpreted "fruitful"; He says: "Ephraim is the helmet of my head." Here He uses the helmet instead of the crown, because what is placed on the head is the wreath. And the Holy Scripture uses many expressions concerning the wreath...

Notice what the psalm says: you have become Gilead, you have become Manasseh, he emigrated to the Lord, and after your forgetfulness you returned to your Father. Be Ephraim also, that is, be fruitful, practicing good works, and afterward you become the crown of the Lord [12].
* "Judah is my sceptre." Think of the greatness of the glory that awaits the penitent; now Judah means "confession" [13].

St. Jerome *The word "Gilead" is interpreted "transfer," "Manasseh" means "forgetfulness," "Ephraim" means "abundance of fruit," and "Judah" is interpreted "the confessor"... This indicates that Christ says after His ascension into heaven: Everyone who has passed from unbelief to faith submits to Me, and whoever has forgotten his former evil works, and whoever bears abundant fruit by working virtues, he rules over the enemies, and the confessor becomes a king like Me... As for the sons of Moab, who were forbidden to enter the temple, they are about to become My own through the washing of holy Baptism.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem
Moab is my washpot;
over Edom will I cast out my shoe;
O Philistia, shout aloud over me [9].
The text in the Septuagint and Coptic versions reads: "Moab is the vessel of my hope".

Moab, together with Edom and Ammon, was among the fiercest enemies of Israel. And the Law came commanding that none of the Moabites and the Amorites should enter the congregation of the Lord until the tenth generation (Deut 23:3-6). But the psalmist, having lifted his eyes to the Cross, saw Moab enjoying the waters of Baptism (the washpot) that belong to the Lord, so that they become sons of God, the object of His pleasure.

Moab, who was the fruit of the sin of Lot with his daughter, a symbol of uncleanness, represents Satan; he enjoyed reconciliation with God, and left his sonship to the devil to live in the bosom of the Lord. This is the chosen vessel for which the Lord hopes by the power of His Cross.

Edom, which means blood or earth, refers to the first Adam, fallen because of his rebellion against God, who enjoyed the descent of the Word of God incarnate, and lives in the midst of mankind that He may unite him to Himself.
As for Philistia, which was in continual resistance to His people, opposing the worship of the true God, when it believes in the crucified Christ it is turned into a chorus of acclamation.
Thus the Church of Christ became the holy Bride from all nations, peoples, and tongues.

Eusebius sees that the shoe refers to the Incarnation; for this reason John the Baptist said that he was not worthy to loose the latchet of His shoe, that is, to explain the mystery of His Incarnation. So over Edom He casts His shoe, that is, the Lord Christ walks with the preaching of His holy Gospel over the Gentile lands and foreign tribes such as Edom, which means earth.

* "Moab is the cauldron (washpot) of my hope." What a great mystery we learn from these few words... For Moab is translated "from the father"... Who is this man who is from the father? He who loses his father, who left him and did not return to him, so he is not worthy to be called Manasseh.
Who is Moab? An enemy of the Lord, whose kind, even to the fourth and tenth generation, indeed to the end of the world, does not enter the Church of the Lord.

Who is Moab? He who is born in the pit of darkness from an unclean union. From the union of Lot with his two daughters two sons were born: Moab is the elder... in the darkness in a cave, and not in the sun and the light; for this reason Moab is the other name of Satan, who does not think of his father. Truly Absalom, who persecuted his father, also represents the devil.
But in what sense is Moab called the washpot of the hope of the Lord...? The Apostle says: "Whom I have delivered unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme" (1 Tim 1:20).
Satan is, as it appears, the Lord's means of discipline. Those who do not walk toward God in righteousness are delivered to Satan... until they return to (the Lord)...

"Over Edom will I cast out my shoe." "Edom" means "from the earth," and "from the blood." The God of love and tenderness lays claim not only to the heavenly but also to the earthly. The Philistines become my friends. He says this about us who believe and were from the Gentiles [14].
St. Jerome *The nation of Moab submits to them, and becomes like a basin for washing their feet, and their feet extend to the land of Edom, and the neighboring foreign nations submit to them.
Father Anthimus of Jerusalem
Who will bring me into the strong city?
Who will lead me into Edom? [10].

The psalmist longs to see the Church of the New Testament, the fortified city, and to be guided to Edom, which had been estranged by its worship of idols and came to bear the preaching of the divine Incarnation. The Lord Himself, the secret of her strength, rejoices in her, saying: "Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?" (Song 6:10).

St. Jerome sees the fortified city as Hades, which whoever enters cannot leave. The men of the Old Testament entered it and could not leave it. It is said of Jacob: "And he refused to be comforted; and he said, For I will go down into the grave unto my son mourning. Thus his father wept for him" (Gen 37:35) (that is, for his son Joseph). Hades had an entrance, but it had no exit. One alone entered Hades and came out victorious, our Lord Jesus Christ!

David the psalmist, like all the men of the Old Testament, feared death, because Hades awaited them, but the Cross of the Lord of glory Jesus shattered the bars of Hades and emptied it of those who died in hope of God's wonderful salvation!
Wilt not thou, O God, who hast cast us off? and wilt not thou, O God, go forth with our hosts? [11].
It is good for a man to work and strive like a mighty army, but without the grace of God he becomes rejected, and it is in vain that he enjoys victory.

God is a refuge for us in the midst of our distress; by His grace He leads all our energies and turns our hearts into a Jerusalem like an army with banners (Song 6:4), which no powers of darkness can storm.

* Notice the prophet's words carefully. He did not say: You go forth, but "and wilt not thou, O God, go forth with our hosts?" The prophet's teaching is this: when we exert effort, God helps us. So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy (Rom 9:16). Do you understand that this saying means: it is not of him who rests, nor of him who sleeps, but of God who shows mercy...? On our part we must will and run; then He has compassion on us. When the wrestler sleeps he loses the victory [15].
St. Jerome
Give us help from trouble:
for vain is the help of man [12].

We often murmur in time of distress, and we even see in the writings of the Fathers, such as the Conferences of St. John Cassian, that one of the Fathers was asked: Why does God allow tribulations for the saints?

Affliction, as St. Augustine sees it, comes by God's permission for our edification, for we do not taste God's mercies and His care for us and touch His love as we do when affliction comes upon us, so we cry out to God and discover that He is a refuge for us in our distress.

* Do you want the Lord to hear you with tenderness? While you are in distress, call upon Him, and He will answer you kindly. Unless a person is in distress he cannot call upon the Lord for help. Vain is the help of men. [Cursed be the man that trusteth in man] (See Jer 17:5) [16].
St. Jerome
Through God we shall do valiantly:
for he it is that shall tread down our enemies [13].

Through the literal Law, man did not enjoy salvation but was in distress; but now that the Word of God has come incarnate, He has given us the spirit of power and of victory over the devil and his angels, our true enemies.

* "Through God we shall do valiantly" [13]. Let us put our trust in God alone... Christ is with you; are you still afraid? If He feeds the birds of heaven, do you doubt His power to feed you also? Does Satan feed his men, and Christ not feed His servants...? Let us cast out all anxiety from our hearts, and say: "Through God we shall do valiantly." He will be our bread, He will be our king. "He it is that shall tread down our enemies." He crowns, He fights with us at our side, and more than this, He wins the victory in us... When we are courageous He treads down our enemies. Scripture did not say that He fights or kills, but that He treads down our enemies [17].
St. Jerome
Your praise fills my whole being with Your glory!
*In the midst of my distress I take refuge in You, for You are the faithful refuge.
My heart is filled with Your peace, and my depths rejoice in You.
And my body sets out to work and service by Your Holy Spirit.
I have truly realized why the heavenly ones live in a feast that never ends!
For You have no need of anyone's praise; rather, praise of You fills the being of Your creation with inexpressible joy!
*I say with the psalmist: My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.
By Your grace my heart has hated all defilement and uncleanness, and has become a royal palace in which You dwell.
You pour upon it from the abundance of Your grace, and the fragrance of Your holiness spreads in it!
You fill it with the treasures of Your glory, and adorn it with Your wondrous splendor!
Allow me to proclaim with all power?
Your indwelling fills my tongue with praise, and overflows with Your glory upon my depths!
You are my glory, my satisfaction, and my unceasing joy!
*As I meditate on Your love, the darkness of night is turned into wondrous light!
The body sleeps and rests, but Your light fills my depths with splendor.
At dawn, at the rising of the sun, I take the psaltery and the harp.
Play upon the strings of my soul that rejoices in You.
For all that is within me finds its delight in praising You!
*By Your incarnation the dawn has come upon us, O Sun of Righteousness.
So our souls, together with our bodies, set out praising You in wondrous harmony.
*By Your becoming man You came down to us; You turned our life into a unique harp, on which You play with the Spirit of divine love, and You grant us the risen life, ever rejoicing and praising.
*How wondrous! The psalmist enjoyed the spirit of prophecy.
He saw You risen to gather the peoples together into Your rejoicing Church.
He went forth to sing to You among the peoples coming to You.
He beheld Your Church having become a new heaven.
So he realized that Your mercy has lifted the earthly ones on high.
Men join with the heavenly orders in praising You.
I proclaim Your glory in men who have become almost heavenly.
They rose up from the dunghill and sat with the upper orders in heaven!
*Your Cross is the fountain of praise and joy.
The Father rejoices and exults, seeing mankind regain its beauty.
Mankind bowed its shoulders and began to praise:
I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.
It enjoyed the knowledge of the mysteries of heaven, each according to his measure.
It emigrated to Him, for it was freed from bondage to the devil.
It returned remembering the kindnesses of its heavenly Father, after having previously forgotten His fatherhood and squandered its inheritance.
It began to confess His mercy and to find its glory in Him.
It was washed in the waters of Baptism, and enjoyed the spirit of adoption.
*By Your Cross You acquired Your Church from all peoples.

From the tribes of Israel, such as Gilead, Manasseh, Ephraim, and Judah, those who emigrated to You, where they understood the prophecies, left the letter of the Law and received it by the life-giving Spirit.
They became kings with authority, over whom the devil, the opponent of the truth, has no power.
From the Gentiles, Moab, Edom, Philistia, and others enjoyed membership in Your holy Body.
The spirit of enmity departed from them and they were kindled with holy zeal.
They left vanities and the worship of idols, and accepted Your true divine Cross.
Your Cross turned Hades into a wondrous spectacle!
We stand before it, which had imprisoned the souls of all, with its gates shattered and its bars collapsed.
Those who were as in an eternal prison came out, rejoicing in You, O Conqueror of Hades and Giver of eternity!
*Your Cross strengthened our arms.
It turned our hearts into the awesome Jerusalem, like an army with banners.
You became the commander of the battle against the devil, and gave us the spirit of power and certainty in Your victory!
We no longer fear the enemy, for the devil falls like lightning from heaven.
You gave us authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy!
Glory to You, O Crucified One, Giver of glory and power!
